The Integrability of New Two-Component
KdV Equation

This paper is a contribution to the Proceedings of the XVIIIth International Colloquium on Integrable Systems and Quantum Symmetries (June 18–20, 2009, Prague, Czech Republic). The full collection is available at http://www.emis.de/journals/SIGMA/ISQS2009.html
Ziemowit POPOWICZ
Abstract

We consider the bi-Hamiltonian representation of the two-component coupled KdV equations discovered by Drinfel’d and Sokolov and rediscovered by Sakovich and Foursov. Connection of this equation with the supersymmetric Kadomtsev–Petviashvilli–Radul–Manin hierarchy is presented. For this new supersymmetric equation the Lax representation and odd Hamiltonian structure is given.

keywords
KdV equation; Lax representation; integrability; supersymmetry

1 Introduction

The scalar KdV equation admits various generalizations to the multifield case and have been often considered in the literature [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. However, the present classification of such systems is not complete and depends on the assumption which we made on the very beginning.

Svinolupov [2] has introduced the class of equations

uti=ux​x​xi+aj,ki​uj​uxk,\displaystyle u^{i}_{t}=u^{i}_{xxx}+a^{i}_{j,k}u^{j}u_{x}^{k}, (1)

where i,j,k=1,2,…,Ni,j,k=1,2,\dots,N, uiu_{i} are functions depending on the variables xx and tt and aj,kia^{i}_{j,k} are constants. The aj,kia^{i}_{j,k} satisfy the same relations as the structural constants of Jordan algebra

aj,kn​(an,rj​am,sr−am,ri​an,sr)+cyclic⁡(j,k,m)=0.\displaystyle a^{n}_{j,k}\big(a^{j}_{n,r}a^{r}_{m,s}-a^{i}_{m,r}a^{r}_{n,s}\big)+{\rm cyclic}(j,k,m)=0.

These equations possess infinitely many higher generalized symmetries.

Gürses and Karasu [3] extended the Svinolupov construction to the system of equations

utj=bji​ux​x​xi+sj,ki​uj​uxk,\displaystyle u^{j}_{t}=b^{i}_{j}u^{i}_{xxx}+s^{i}_{j,k}u^{j}u^{k}_{x}, (2)

where bjib^{i}_{j}, sj,kis^{i}_{j,k} are constants.

In general, existence of infinitely many conserved quantities is admitted as the definition of integrability. This implies existence of infinitely many generalized symmetries. Gürses and Karasu, in order to check the integrability of the system of equations (2), assumed that the system is integrable if it admits a recursion operator. Assuming the general form of the second and fourth order recursion operator they found the conditions on the coefficients bjib^{i}_{j}, sj,kis^{i}_{j,k} so that the equations in (2) are integrable.

A quite different generalization of multicomponent KdV system has been found by Antonowicz and Fordy [4] considering the energy dependent Schrödinger operator. Ma [5] also presented a multicomponent KdV system considering decomposable hereditary operators.

Several years ago Foursov [6] found the conditions on the coefficients bjib^{i}_{j}, sj,kis^{i}_{j,k} under which the two-component system (2) possesses at least 5 generalized symmetries and conserved quantities. He carried out computer algebra computations and found that there are five such systems which are not symmetrical and not triangular. Three of them are known to be integrable, while two of them are new. Foursov conjectured that these two new systems should be integrable. However, it appeared that one of these new systems is not new and has been known for many years. Drinfel’d and Sokolov in 1981 [7] presented the Lax pair for one of these new equation and hence this equation is integrable.

In this paper we present the bi-Hamiltonian formulation and recursion operator for the new equation. These results have been obtained during the study of the so called supersymmetric Manin–Radul hierarchy. The application of the supersymmetry to the construction of new integrable systems appeared almost in parallel to the use of this symmetry in the quantum field theory. The quantum field theories with exact correspondences between bosonic and fermionic helicity states are not the only basic ingredients for superstring theories, but have been utilised both in theoretical and experimental research in particle physics. The first results, concerned the construction of classical field theories with fermionic and bosonic fields depending on time and one space variable, can be found in [8, 9, 10, 11]. In many cases, addition of fermion fields does not guarantee that the final theory becomes supersymmetric invariant. Therefore this method was named as a fermionic extension in order to distinguish it from the fully supersymmetrical method which was developed later [12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. There are many recipes how some classical models could be embedded in fully supersymmetric superspace. The main idea is simple: in order to get such generalization we should construct a supermultiplet containing the classical functions. It means that we have to add to a system of kk bosonic equations k​NkN fermions and k⁡(N−1)k(N-1) bosons (k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dots, N=1,2,…N=1,2,\dots) in such a way that they create superfields. Now working with this supermultiplet we can step by step apply integrable Hamiltonians methods to our considerations depending on what we would like to construct.

Manin and Radul in 1985 [11], introduced a new system of equations for an infinite set of even and odd functions, depending on an even-odd pair of space variables and even-odd times. This system of equations now called the Manin–Radul supersymmetric Kadomtsev–Petviashvili hierarchy (MR-SKP). It appeared that this hierarchy contains the supersymmetric generalization of the Korteweg–de Vries equation, the Sawada–Kotera equation and as we show in this paper two-component coupled KdV equations discovered by Drinfel’d–Sokolov.

2 Two-component KdV systems

Let us consider a system of two equations

ut=F⁡[u,v],vt=G⁡[u,v],\displaystyle u_{t}=F[u,v],\qquad v_{t}=G[u,v],

where F⁡[u,v]=F⁡(u,v,ux,vx,…)F[u,v]=F(u,v,u_{x},v_{x},\dots) denotes a differential polynomial function of uu and vv.

By the triangular system we understand such system which involves either an equation depending only on uu or an equation depending only on vv while by the symmetrical we understand such system in which G⁡[u,v]=F⁡[v,u]G[u,v]=F[v,u].

Definition 2.1.

A system of tt-independent evolution equations

ut=Q1​[u,v],vt=Q2​[u,v]\displaystyle u_{t}=Q_{1}[u,v],\qquad v_{t}=Q_{2}[u,v]

is said to be a generalized symmetry of (1) if their flows formally commute

𝐃𝐊​(𝐐)−𝐃𝐐​(𝐊)=𝟎.\displaystyle{\bf D}_{\bf K}({\bf Q})-{\bf D}_{{\bf Q}}({\bf K})={\bf 0}.

Here 𝐐=(Q1,Q2){\bf Q}=(Q_{1},Q_{2}), 𝐊⁡[u,v]=(F⁡[u,v],G⁡[u,v]){\bf K}[u,v]=(F[u,v],G[u,v]), and 𝐃𝐊{\bf D}_{\bf K} denotes the Fréchet derivative.

The first three systems in the Foursov classification are known to be integrable equations and are

ut=ux​x​x+6​u​ux−12​v​vx,\displaystyle u_{t}=u_{xxx}+6uu_{x}-12vv_{x},
vt=−2​vx​x​x−6​u​vx;\displaystyle v_{t}=-2v_{xxx}-6uv_{x};
ut=ux​x​x+3​u​ux+3​v​vx,\displaystyle u_{t}=u_{xxx}+3uu_{x}+3vv_{x},
vt=ux​v+u​vx;\displaystyle v_{t}=u_{x}v+uv_{x};
ut=ux​x​x+2​v​ux+u​vx,\displaystyle u_{t}=u_{xxx}+2vu_{x}+uv_{x},
vt=u​ux.\displaystyle v_{t}=uu_{x}.

The first pair of equations is the Hirota–Satsuma system [17], second is the Ito system [18], third is the rescaled Drinfel’d–Sokolov equation [6].

The fourth system of equations is a new one founded by Foursov

ut=ux​x​x+vx​x​x+2​v​ux+2​u​vx,\displaystyle u_{t}=u_{xxx}+v_{xxx}+2vu_{x}+2uv_{x},
vt=vx​x​x−9​u​ux+6​v​ux+3​u​vx+2​v​vx.\displaystyle v_{t}=v_{xxx}-9uu_{x}+6vu_{x}+3uv_{x}+2vv_{x}.

Foursov showed that this system possesses generalized symmetries of weights 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19, as well as conserved densities of weights 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14, and conjectured that this system is integrable and should possess infinitely many generalized symmetries.

The last system in this classification is

ut=4​ux​x​x+3​vx​x​x+4​u​ux+v​ux+2​u​vx,\displaystyle u_{t}=4u_{xxx}+3v_{xxx}+4uu_{x}+vu_{x}+2uv_{x},
vt=3​ux​x​x+vx​x​x−4​v​ux−2​u​vx−2​v​vx,\displaystyle v_{t}=3u_{xxx}+v_{xxx}-4vu_{x}-2uv_{x}-2vv_{x}, (3)

and has been first considered many years ago by Drinfel’d and Sokolov [7] and rediscovered by S.Yu. Sakovich [19].

Let us notice that the integrable Hirota–Satsuma equation has the following Lax representation [20]

L=(∂2+u+v)(∂2+u−v),∂L∂t=4[L+3/4,L],\displaystyle L=\big(\partial^{2}+u+v\big)\big(\partial^{2}+u-v\big),\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}=4\big[L^{3/4}_{+},L\big],

while the integrable Drinfel’d–Sokolov equation possesses the following Lax representation [3, 21]

L=(∂3+(u−v)∂+(ux−vx)/2)(∂3+(u+v)∂+(ux+vx)/2),∂L∂t=4[L+3/4,L].\displaystyle L=\big(\partial^{3}+(u-v)\partial+(u_{x}-v_{x})/2\big)\big(\partial^{3}+(u+v)\partial+(u_{x}+v_{x})/2\big),\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}=4\big[L^{3/4}_{+},L\big].

On the other side, the Lax operators of the Hirota–Satsuma equation and of the Drinfel’d–Sokolov equation could be considered as special reduced Lax operators of the fourth and sixth order respectively. Indeed, the Hirota–Satsuma Lax operator could be rewritten as

L=∂4+g2∂2+g1∂+g0,\displaystyle L=\partial^{4}+g_{2}\partial^{2}+g_{1}\partial+g_{0}, (4)

where

g2=2​u,g1=2​(ux−vx),g0=ux​x+u2−vx​x−v2.\displaystyle g_{2}=2u,\qquad g_{1}=2(u_{x}-v_{x}),\qquad g_{0}=u_{xx}+u^{2}-v_{xx}-v^{2}.

In this context, one can ask what kind of the equations follows from the fifth-order Lax operator which is parametrised by two functions of same weight. Let us therefore consider the following Lax operator

L=∂5+h2∂3+h3∂2+h4∂+h5,\displaystyle L=\partial^{5}+h_{2}\partial^{3}+h_{3}\partial^{2}+h_{4}\partial+h_{5},

where hih_{i}, i=2,3,4,5i=2,3,4,5 are polynomials in uu and vv and their derivatives of the dimension ii. Computing the Lax representation for this operator

∂L∂t=5​[L,L+3/5]\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}=5\big[L,L^{3/5}_{+}\big]

we obtained then

L=(∂3+23u∂+13ux)(∂2−13v)\displaystyle L=\big(\partial^{3}+\tfrac{2}{3}u\partial+\tfrac{1}{3}u_{x}\big)\big(\partial^{2}-\tfrac{1}{3}v\big) (5)

produces the system of equation (3).

Let us notice that the Lax operator (4) is factorized as the product of two Lax operators. The first one is the Lax operator of the Kaup–Kupershmidt equation while the second is the Lax operator of the Korteweg–de Vries equation. It is exactly the same Lax operator which has been found by Drinfel’d and Sokolov [7].

Hence we encounter the situation in which the Lax operator of the Korteweg–de Vries and the Kaup–Kupershmidt equations can be used for construction of additional equations. This could be schematically presented as:

\tsep4pt L~KdV\tilde{L}_{\rm KdV} L~KK\tilde{L}_{\rm KK} \bsep2pt \tsep4pt LKdVL_{\rm KdV} Hirota–Satsuma equations (3) \bsep2pt \tsep4pt LKKL_{\rm KK} equations (3) Drinfel’d–Sokolov \bsep2pt

where LKdVL_{\rm KdV}, L~Kdv\tilde{L}_{\rm Kdv} are two different Lax operators of the Korteweg–de Vries equation while LKKL_{\rm KK} and L~KK\tilde{L}_{\rm KK} are two different Lax operators of the Kaup–Kupershmidt equation.

4 The derivation of the Lax representation

The Lax operator of equations (5) has been discovered accidentally during the investigations of the supersymmetric Manin–Radul hierarchy. This hierarchy can be described by the supersymmetric Lax operator

L=𝒟+f0+∑j=1∞bj∂−j𝒟+∑j=1∞fj∂−j,\displaystyle L={\cal D}+f_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}b_{j}\partial^{-j}{\cal D}+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}f_{j}\partial^{-j}, (6)

where the coefficients bjb_{j}, fjf_{j} are bosonic and fermionic superfield functions, respectively. We shall use the following notation throughout the paper: ∂\partial and 𝒟=∂∂θ+θ∂{\cal D}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}+\theta\partial. As usual, (x,θ)(x,\theta) denotes N=1N=1 superspace coordinates. For any super pseudodifferential operator 𝒜=∑jaj/2​𝒟j{\cal A}=\sum\limits_{j}a_{j/2}{\cal D}^{j} the subscripts ±\pm denote its purely differential part 𝒜+=∑j≥0aj/2​𝒟j{\cal A}_{+}=\sum\limits_{j\geq 0}a_{j/2}{\cal D}^{j} or its purely pseudo-differential part 𝒜−=∑j≥1a−j/2𝒟−j{\cal A}_{-}=\sum\limits_{j\geq 1}a_{-j/2}{\cal D}^{-j} respectively. For any 𝒜{\cal A} the super-residuum is defined as Res𝒜=a−1/2{\rm Res}\,{\cal A}=a_{-1/2}.

The constrained (r,m)(r,m) supersymmetric Manin–Radul hierarchy [26] is defined by the following Lax operator

L=𝒟r+∑j=0r−1Ψj/2​𝒟j+∑j=0mΥm−j2​𝒟−1​Ψj/2.\displaystyle L={\cal D}^{r}+\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\Psi_{j/2}{\cal D}^{j}+\sum_{j=0}^{m}\Upsilon_{\frac{m-j}{2}}{\cal D}^{-1}\Psi_{j/2}.

This hierarchy for even rr has been widely studied in the literature in contrast to the odd rr which is less known. Further we will consider this hierarchy for odd r=3,5r=3,5 and m=0m=0, Υ=Ψ=0\Upsilon=\Psi=0.

The Lax operator for r=3r=3 and m=0m=0, Υ=Ψ=0\Upsilon=\Psi=0 has been considered recently by Tian and Liu [25]

L=𝒟3+Φ,\displaystyle L={\cal D}^{3}+\Phi,

where Φ\Phi is a superfermion function. Let us consider the following tower of equations

Lt,k=9​[L,L+k/3].\displaystyle L_{t,k}=9\big[L,L^{k/3}_{+}\big].

The first four consistent nontrivial equations are

Φt,2=Φx,\displaystyle\Phi_{t,2}=\Phi_{x},
Φτ,7=(Φ1,x​x+12​Φ12+3​Φ​Φx)x,\displaystyle\Phi_{\tau,7}=\big(\Phi_{1,xx}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Phi_{1}^{2}+3\Phi\Phi_{x}\big)_{x},
Φt,10=Φ5​x+5​Φx​x​x​Φ1+5​Φx​x​Φ1,x+5​Φx​Φ12,\displaystyle\Phi_{t,10}=\Phi_{5x}+5\Phi_{xxx}\Phi_{1}+5\Phi_{xx}\Phi_{1,x}+5\Phi_{x}\Phi_{1}^{2},
Φτ,11=Φ1,5​x+3​Φ1,x​x​x​Φ1+6​Φ1,x​x​Φ1,x+2​Φ1,x​Φ12\displaystyle\Phi_{\tau,11}=\Phi_{1,5x}+3\Phi_{1,xxx}\Phi_{1}+6\Phi_{1,xx}\Phi_{1,x}+2\Phi_{1,x}\Phi_{1}^{2}
−3​Φ4​x​Φ−2​Φx​x​x​Φx−6​Φx​x​Φ​Φ1−6​Φx​Φ​Φ1,x,\displaystyle\phantom{\Phi_{\tau,11}=}{}-3\Phi_{4x}\Phi-2\Phi_{xxx}\Phi_{x}-6\Phi_{xx}\Phi\Phi_{1}-6\Phi_{x}\Phi\Phi_{1,x},

where tt is a usual time while τ\tau is an odd time.

The third equation in the hierarchy in the component Φ=ξ+θ​w\Phi=\xi+\theta w reads

ξt=ξ5​x+5​w​ξx​x​x+5​wx​ξx​x+5​u2​ξx,\displaystyle\xi_{t}=\xi_{5x}+5w\xi_{xxx}+5w_{x}\xi_{xx}+5u^{2}\xi_{x},
wt=w5​x+5​w​wx​x​x+5​wx​wx​x+5​w2​wx−5​ξx​x​x​ξx\displaystyle w_{t}=w_{5x}+5ww_{xxx}+5w_{x}w_{xx}+5w^{2}w_{x}-5\xi_{xxx}\xi_{x}

and it is a supersymmetric generalization of the Sawada–Kotera equation. This equation is a bi-Hamiltonian system with odd supersymmetric Poisson brackets [24]. The proper Hamiltonian operator which satisfies the Jacobi identity and generates the supersymmetric N=1N=1 Sawada–Kotera equation is

Φt,10=P​δ​H1δ​Φ,\displaystyle\Phi_{t,10}=P\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\Phi},

where H1=∫Φ​Φx​𝑑x​𝑑θH_{1}=\int\Phi\Phi_{x}\,dxd\theta and

P=(𝒟∂2+2∂Φ+2Φ∂+𝒟Φ𝒟)∂−1(𝒟∂2+2∂Φ+2Φ∂+𝒟Φ𝒟).\displaystyle P=\big({\cal D}\partial^{2}+2\partial\Phi+2\Phi\partial+{\cal D}\Phi{\cal D}\big)\partial^{-1}\big({\cal D}\partial^{2}+2\partial\Phi+2\Phi\partial+{\cal D}\Phi{\cal D}\big).

The implectic operator for this equation was defined in [24] as

JΦt=δ​H3δ​Φ,J=∂x​x+(𝒟Φ)−∂−1(𝒟Φ)x+∂−1Φx𝒟+Φx∂−1𝒟,\displaystyle J\Phi_{t}=\frac{\delta H_{3}}{\delta\Phi},\qquad J=\partial_{xx}+({\cal D}\Phi)-\partial^{-1}({\cal D}\Phi)_{x}+\partial^{-1}\Phi_{x}{\cal D}+\Phi_{x}\partial^{-1}{\cal D}, (7)

where

H3=∫d​x​𝑑θ​(Φ7​x​Φ+8​Φx​x​x​Φ​(𝒟​Φ)x​x+Φx​Φ​(4​(𝒟​Φ)4​xCLOSECLOSE\displaystyle H_{3}=\int dxd\theta\big(\Phi_{7x}\Phi+8\Phi_{xxx}\Phi({\cal D}\Phi)_{xx}+\Phi_{x}\Phi(4({\cal D}\Phi)_{4x}
OPENOPEN+20​(𝒟​Φ)x​x​(𝒟​Φ)+10​(𝒟​Φ)x2+83​(𝒟​Φ)3)).\displaystyle\phantom{H_{3}=}{}+20({\cal D}\Phi)_{xx}({\cal D}\Phi)+10({\cal D}\Phi)_{x}^{2}+\tfrac{8}{3}({\cal D}\Phi)^{3})\big).

This supersymmetric equation possesses an infinite number of conserved charges [25] which are generated by the supertrace formula of the Lax operator. However, these charges are not reduced to the known conserved charges in the bosonic limit. Hence we can not in general conclude that from the supersymmetric integrability follow the integrability of the bosonic sector.

Let us now consider the Lax operator (6) for r=5r=5 and m=0m=0

L=𝒟5+13(∂U+U∂)−13𝒟V𝒟,\displaystyle L={\cal D}^{5}+\tfrac{1}{3}(\partial U+U\partial)-\tfrac{1}{3}{\cal D}V{\cal D},

where UU and VV are superfermionic functions U=ξ+θ​uU=\xi+\theta u, V=ψ+θ​vV=\psi+\theta v. The first nontrivial equations in the hierarchy generated by this Lax operator is given as

Lt=[L+6/5,L],\displaystyle L_{t}=\big[L^{6/5}_{+},L\big],
Ut=4​Ux​x​x+3​Vx​x​x−2​Ux​(𝒟​U+𝒟​V)+U⁡(6​𝒟​Ux+2​𝒟​Vx)−Vx​𝒟​V+V⁡(3​𝒟​Ux+𝒟​Vx),\displaystyle U_{t}=4U_{xxx}+3V_{xxx}-2U_{x}({\cal D}U+{\cal D}V)+U(6{\cal D}U_{x}+2{\cal D}V_{x})-V_{x}{\cal D}V+V(3{\cal D}U_{x}+{\cal D}V_{x}),
Vt=3​Ux​x​x+Vx​x​x+8​Ux​𝒟​U−U⁡(8​𝒟​Ux−6​𝒟​Vx)+Vx​(4​𝒟​U+𝒟​V)−V⁡(4​𝒟​Ux+3​𝒟​Vx).\displaystyle V_{t}=3U_{xxx}+V_{xxx}+8U_{x}{\cal D}U-U(8{\cal D}U_{x}-6{\cal D}V_{x})+V_{x}(4{\cal D}U+{\cal D}V)-V(4{\cal D}U_{x}+3{\cal D}V_{x}).

The bosonic sector of the latter system where ξ=0\xi=0, ψ=0\psi=0 gives us the system of two interacted KdV type equations discovered by Drinfel’d–Sokolov.

Interestingly, the Lax operator equations (7) did not reduce in the bosonic sector to our Lax operator (5), however, its second power reduces that one can easy verify. As we checked, this system possesses the same properties as the supersymmetric Sawada–Kotera equation. Namely, this model, due to the Lax representation, has an infinite number of conserved quantities, which are not reduced to the usual conserved charges in the bosonic limit. For example, the first two conserved charges are

H1=∫d​x​𝑑θ​(4​Ux​U+6​Vx​V+Vx​V),\displaystyle H_{1}=\int dxd{\theta}(4U_{x}U+6V_{x}V+V_{x}V),
H2=∫d​x​𝑑θ​(75​Ux​x​x​U+32​Ux​U​(𝒟​U)−24​Ux​U​(𝒟​V)+90​Vx​x​x​U+30​Vx​x​x​VCLOSE\displaystyle H_{2}=\int dxd{\theta}\big(75U_{xxx}U+32U_{x}U({\cal D}U)-24U_{x}U({\cal D}V)+90V_{xxx}U+30V_{xxx}V
OPEN+36​Vx​U​(𝒟​U)−6​Vx​U​(𝒟​V)−4​Vx​V​(𝒟​V)−30​V​U​(𝒟​Vx)).\displaystyle\phantom{H_{2}=}{}+36V_{x}U({\cal D}U)-6V_{x}U({\cal D}V)-4V_{x}V({\cal D}V)-30VU({\cal D}V_{x})\big). (8)

We found the following odd Hamiltonian structure for our supersymmetric equation (8)

dd​t​(UV)=(130110−110−215)​(δ​H2δ​uδ​H2δ​v).\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}U\\ V\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{1}{30}&\frac{1}{10}\\ -\frac{1}{10}&-\frac{2}{15}\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\dfrac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta u}\\ \dfrac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta v}\end{array}\right).

Unfortunately, we have been not able to found second Hamiltonian structure for our superequation.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
